slides: So, before you practice, here's a quick review of the whole topic.
The signs, the remainder rules, the tools... and the traps.
You want to know when a number divides... without actually dividing.
Now, eleven. You alternate plus and minus, digit by digit.
A bigger divisor? Split it into parts with no common factor.
Four and six share a two. So that check proves nothing.
A fraction of a fraction? Build it from the inside.
Multiply the denominators. So the number is divisible by eighteen.
Because, well... there's no such thing as a third of a student.
The remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
So dividing by nine? The remainder is at most eight.
Four thousand eight hundred twenty-six. The digit sum is twenty, so it leaves two when you divide by nine.
Only the leftovers matter.
Add, multiply, or subtract the remainders. If you get a negative? Add the divisor.
And if you take away the remainder, what's left divides exactly.
A new divisor? Check that it divides the old one.
Four divides twelve. So keep the remainder... and divide it again if it's too big.
But four doesn't divide ten. You get two answers, so you can't know.
How many multiples? Look at the first and the last.
And don't forget the plus one. Both ends count.
Now, powers repeat every four steps.
Numbers in a row hide everywhere.
But only IN A ROW. n times n plus two is not.
One value that fails knocks out a choice. But values that work prove nothing.

And the traps. Twenty-four is not four times six, and counting forgets the plus one.
Well... you know all of this. Go practice.
